title: Super lobby pushes back on cold-call ban
full_text:
The Association of Superannuation Funds of Australia has urged the federal government to put super-related lead generation under the financial services umbrella rather than impose an outright ban on the murky cold-calling industry.
Speaking after The Australian revealed Assistant Treasurer Daniel Mulino is leaning towards outlawing cold calling in super, ASFA chief executive Mary Delahunty said forcing lead generators to be licensed would keep them under the gaze of the corporate cop.
“Lead generators are clearly hanging around in the dark areas of the system. It’s a low-margin business. So anything that the government can do to make compliance costly will likely force those lead generators to not have a business any more,” Ms Delahunty said.
An outright ban on super lead generation risked removing elements that were useful to consumers, she added.
“I do believe in licensing (lead generators). I think you have to back in the licensing regime because that would then protect useful consumer information,” Ms Delahunty said.
“If the minister instead wants to pursue a banning of lead generation, we’ll work with him to make sure that we can have a clear definition of what that is.” Ahead of his first National Press Club address on August 19, Dr Mulino is finalising reforms to protect Australians from dodgy superannuation operators in the wake of two investment scheme collapses that cost 11,000 Australians $1bn in super.
The reforms are the government’s solution to plugging the gaping holes that led to the collapse of the Shield Master Fund and the First Guardian Master Fund. They are the result of months of consultation with regulators, industry and consumer groups.
Shield and First Guardian were two failed managed investment schemes that grew at a rapid clip over a few years due to high-pressure sales tactics by cold callers and lead generators. Both funds are now in liquidation and under investigation by the Australian Securities and Investments Commission.
The scandal exposed deep flaws in the regulation of Australia’s $4.5 trillion retirement nest egg, with alleged failures all along the investment chain, from the ratings houses to the advisers, the super trustees and the funds themselves.
After consulting with regulators, industry and consumer advocates, the government is understood to be leaning toward a ban on unsolicited approaches about a person’s super.
The Council of Australian Life Insurers urged the government to take a narrow approach to a ban on lead generation to avoid unintended consequences.
“Life insurance lead generation plays an important role in helping customers access information, compare products and obtain life insurance protection,” said CALI chief executive Christine Cupitt.
“Australians need easier access to life insurance, not more barriers. One in two Australians want personalised advice about life insurance, and more people are turning to online tools, including market comparison sites, to learn about life insurance.
“The government should not cut off safe, regulated pathways that help Australians access the protection they need.” The council does not support cold calling or high-pressure sales practices, she added.
ASFA’s Ms Delahunty also called for the government to put the Compensation Scheme of Last Resort on more solid footing, including by directing ASIC penalties to the under-pressure scheme.
“It doesn’t meet ordinary community expectations if there are penalties that completely drain a wrongdoer’s assets or cash and those penalties go into government general revenue rather than be paid to victims,” she said.
“With its really wide-ranging powers, we’ve been encouraging the regulator to be seeking cost orders (rather than penalties) in order to bring the victim compensation closer.” Dr Mulino is expected to announce changes to the CSLR, including removing the controversial ‘but for’ provision that sees victims of financial misconduct compensated for hypothetical losses. The CSLR hands up to $150,000 in compensation to victims of financial misconduct when the responsible firm is insolvent.
